questions.stem: What does 「せいかく」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「せいかく」 is a person's character: 「明るいせいかくです」 is 'has a cheerful personality'. Appearance is 「見た目」, a relationship 「かんけい」 and health 「けんこう」.

questions.stem: What does 「生活」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「生活」 (せいかつ) is everyday life or lifestyle: 「日本の生活」 is life in Japan. It shares 「生」 with 「学生」, a student, and 「活」 with 「活動」, an activity, which makes those the tempting misreadings.

questions.stem: What does 「けんこうのために、毎朝歩いています。」 mean?
options: I walk every morning because I am ill.
I want to walk every morning for my health.
I walked every morning when I was healthy.
I walk every morning for my health.
questions.explanation: Noun + 「のために」 gives a purpose, 'for the sake of', and 「歩いています」 is a habit, 'I walk'. Wanting to walk would be 「歩きたいです」, and nothing in the sentence is past.

questions.stem: What does 「ストレスがたまる」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「たまる」 is to pile up or accumulate, so stress is building up: 「しけんの前はストレスがたまります」. Getting rid of stress is 「ストレスをかいしょうする」, the opposite.

questions.stem: What does 「私は好ききらいが多いです。」 mean?
options: I have a lot of friends.
questions.explanation: 「好ききらい」 is likes and dislikes, used above all of food, so having many is being fussy. Liking almost everything is the opposite, and eating too much is 「食べすぎる」.

questions.stem: Read the post: 「私はメルボルンで生まれましたが、りょうしんは日本人です。家では日本語を話して、学校では英語を使います。時々、自分はどちらの国の人なのか分からなくなります。」 What does the writer say?
options: She speaks Japanese at school and English at home
She wants to move to Japan to live with her parents
She sometimes isn't sure where she belongs
She doesn't know which country her parents are from
questions.explanation: 「時々…分からなくなります」 is 'sometimes I stop being sure', and 「どちらの国の人なのか」 is 'which country's person I am'. Her parents are clearly Japanese, and the languages are the other way round: Japanese 「家では」, English 「学校では」.

questions.stem: Read: 「夜おそくまでスマホを見ていたので、朝おきられませんでした。」 Why couldn't the writer get up?
options: He went to bed early but slept badly
He had to work late the night before
He was on his phone until late
His alarm on his phone did not go off
questions.explanation: 「ので」 gives the reason: looking at his phone 「夜おそくまで」, until late at night. 「おきられませんでした」 is the potential, 'couldn't get up'; nothing is said about an alarm or work.

questions.stem: What does 「姉となかがいいです。」 mean?
options: I look like my older sister.
I live with my older sister.
I often argue with my older sister.
I get on well with my older sister.
questions.explanation: 「〜となかがいい」 is to be on good terms with someone. Looking alike is 「にている」, and arguing is 「けんかする」, the opposite of 「なかがいい」.

questions.stem: What does 「けんかする」 mean?
options: to make up after a fight
questions.explanation: 「弟とよくけんかします」 is 'I often fight with my younger brother'. Making up afterwards is 「なかなおりする」 and apologising is 「あやまる」.

questions.stem: What does 「そふぼ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「そふぼ」 combines 「そふ」, grandfather, and 「そぼ」, grandmother. Parents are 「りょうしん」, relatives 「しんせき」 and brothers and sisters 「きょうだい」.

questions.stem: What does 「毎日、犬のせわをします。」 mean?
options: I play with the dog every day.
I wash the dog every day.
I look after the dog every day.
I take the dog for a walk every day.
questions.explanation: 「せわをする」 is to take care of someone or something. Walking the dog is 「犬のさんぽをする」 and washing it 「犬を洗う」, which are particular jobs rather than looking after it in general.

questions.stem: In a Japanese school club, who is your 「せんぱい」?
options: A classmate in your own year
A student in a year above you
A student in a year below you
The teacher who runs the club
questions.explanation: 「せんぱい」 are seniors, and you speak to them politely; juniors are 「こうはい」. The teacher in charge of a club is 「こもん」 or 「こもんの先生」.

questions.stem: Read: 「去年からそふがいっしょに住んでいます。はじめはへやがせまくてたいへんでしたが、今はそふが日曜日にりょうりを作ってくれて、とてもうれしいです。」 How has living together changed?
options: She now cooks for her grandfather on Sundays
It was hard at first, but now she is happy
It was fun at first, but now it is cramped
Her grandfather has moved out again
questions.explanation: 「はじめは…たいへんでした」 is 'at first it was hard', and 「が、今は」 turns to the good side. 「作ってくれて」 means the grandfather cooks for her; cooking for him would be 「作ってあげて」.

questions.stem: Read: 「となりの山田さんは、私たちが旅行に行く時、いつも犬にえさをやってくれます。」 What does this tell you?
options: The neighbour takes the family's dog on holiday
The family takes the dog with them when they travel
The neighbour feeds their dog while they are away
The family feeds the neighbour's dog while the neighbour is away
questions.explanation: 「〜てくれます」 is a favour done for the speaker's side, so 山田さん, the neighbour, feeds the family's dog. 「旅行に行く時」 gives the time: whenever the family goes on a trip.

questions.stem: What does 「アルバイト」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「アルバイト」, often 「バイト」, is casual or part-time work, such as at a 「コンビニ」. A full-time employee is 「せいしゃいん」, and volunteering is 「ボランティア」.

questions.stem: How do you say 'job' in Japanese?
questions.explanation: 「仕事」 (しごと) is work or a job: 「父の仕事はエンジニアです」. 「会社」 is a company and 「社会」, with the same two kanji reversed, is society.

questions.stem: What does 「しょうらいのゆめ」 mean?
options: a dream I had last night
questions.explanation: 「しょうらい」 is the future, so 「しょうらいのゆめ」 is what you hope to become: 「しょうらいのゆめは 先生になることです」. Last night's dream would be 「きのうの夜見たゆめ」, and a memory is 「思い出」.

questions.stem: What does 「しゅうしょくする」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「しゅうしょく」 is taking up employment. Starting at a school or university is 「にゅうがく」, graduating 「そつぎょう」 and retiring 「たいしょく」.

questions.stem: What does 「めんせつ」 mean?
questions.explanation: 「めんせつ」 is a face-to-face interview, for a job or for entry to a school. A résumé is 「りれきしょ」 and an entrance exam 「にゅうし」.

questions.stem: What is 「じゅく」?
options: A school trip taken in the final year
A part-time job at a restaurant
questions.explanation: Many students go to 「じゅく」, a cram school, in the evening to prepare for entrance exams. School clubs are 「ぶかつ」, and a school trip is 「しゅうがくりょこう」.

questions.stem: In Japan, what is 「しゅうかつ」?
options: Club activities held after school each day
Study for high school entrance exams
Training given to new staff at a company
questions.explanation: 「しゅうかつ」 is short for 「しゅうしょくかつどう」, job-hunting activities. Students usually begin it before they graduate. After-school clubs are 「ぶかつ」, from 「ぶかつどう」.

questions.stem: What does 「高校をそつぎょうしたら、大学でかんきょうについて勉強したいと思っています。」 mean?
options: After high school, I'd like to study the environment at university.
I am studying the environment at university after high school.
I graduated from university and now study the environment.
I think high schools should teach students more about the environment.
questions.explanation: 「〜たら」 here is 'after/when', and 「勉強したいと思っています」 is 'I'm thinking I'd like to study'. It is a plan, not something already happening, and the speaker is still at high school.

questions.stem: Read: 「私はコンビニでアルバイトをしています。じきゅうはあまり高くないけれど、いろいろな人と話せるし、お金のたいせつさも分かりました。」 How does the writer feel about the job?
options: She enjoys it but wants to quit soon
She finds talking to customers too hard
The pay is low, but the job has other rewards
The pay is good, so she puts up with dull work
questions.explanation: 「じきゅうはあまり高くないけれど」 is 'the hourly pay isn't very high, but'. Then 「〜し」 lists two gains: talking to all sorts of people and learning the value of money.

questions.stem: What does 「ために」 express in 「いしゃになるために、毎日勉強しています。」?
options: Reason: because she is already a doctor
Time: while she is working as a doctor
Condition: if she ever becomes a doctor
Purpose: in order to become a doctor
questions.explanation: Plain verb + 「ために」 gives the goal the action works towards. A reason would use 「から」 or 「ので」, and a condition 「〜たら」 or 「〜ば」.

questions.stem: Which sentence says 'I have to study tonight'?
options: 今晩勉強してはいけません。
今晩勉強したほうがいいです。
今晩勉強しなければなりません。
今晩勉強しなくてもいいです。
questions.explanation: 「〜なければなりません」 is obligation, 'must'. 「〜なくてもいい」 is 'don't have to', 「〜てはいけません」 is 'must not', and 「〜たほうがいい」 is only advice, 'had better'.

questions.stem: In a Japanese conversation, what are 「あいづち」?
options: Polite ways of turning down an invitation
Questions asked to change the subject
Short replies that show you're listening
Set greetings used to open a conversation
questions.explanation: Listeners say 「はい」, 「ええ」, 「そうですか」 or 「なるほど」 often while the other person talks. Silence can sound as if you are not following, so あいづち keep a conversation going.

questions.stem: Which of these is used as あいづち while someone is telling you something?
options: 「どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
questions.explanation: 「へえ、そうなんですか」 shows interest and surprise, 'oh, really?'. 「どうぞよろしくおねがいします」 belongs to introductions, 「では、また」 closes a conversation, and 「いただきます」 is said before eating.

questions.stem: Your friend says 「きのう、さいふをなくしちゃったんだ。」 Which response fits?
questions.explanation: Losing a wallet is bad news, so 「たいへんだったね」, 'that must have been awful', shows sympathy. 「よかったね」 is for good news, and 「どういたしまして」 answers thanks.

questions.stem: You want to ask a stranger the way. Which phrase opens the conversation politely?
questions.explanation: 「あのう」 is a gentle hesitation and 「すみません」 gets attention, 'excuse me'. 「おかげさまで」 answers a question about how you are, and 「おじゃましました」 is said on leaving a home.

questions.stem: In a conversation, which word changes the topic, like 'by the way'?
questions.explanation: 「ところで」 moves to a new subject: 「ところで、日曜日は何をしましたか。」 「だから」 is 'so', 「それに」 'besides' and 「たとえば」 'for example', which all continue the same topic.

questions.stem: You didn't hear what your host mother said. Which phrase asks her to say it again?
options: 「紙に書いてくださいませんか。」
「もういちど言ってくださいませんか。」
「ゆっくり話してくださいませんか。」
「英語で言ってくださいませんか。」
questions.explanation: 「もういちど」 is 'one more time'. The others ask her to speak slowly, to say it in English or to write it down, which are different requests.

questions.stem: How do you politely end a phone call with your teacher?
questions.explanation: 「しつれいします」 is the polite way to take your leave, on the phone or leaving a room. 「じゃあね、バイバイ」 is for friends, 「もしもし」 opens a call, and 「いってきます」 is said on leaving home.

questions.stem: Which reply disagrees politely with a classmate's opinion?
options: 「私もそう思います。そのとおりですね。」
「なるほど。たしかにそうですね。」
「ほんとうに、私も同じ考えです。」
「そうかもしれませんが、私はちょっとちがうと思います。」
questions.explanation: 「そうかもしれませんが」 grants the point first, and 「ちょっとちがう」 softens the disagreement. The other three all agree: 「同じ考え」 is 'the same opinion'.

questions.stem: Your host father asks 「もっと食べる？」 and you are full. Which reply is polite?
options: 「ありがとうございます。でも、もうおなかがいっぱいです。」
「いいえ、もう食べたくないです。」
「いいえ、あまりおいしくないです。」
questions.explanation: Thanking first and giving a reason, 'I'm already full', declines without seeming to refuse the food. 「食べたくないです」 is blunt, and 「いただきます」 would accept more.

questions.stem: At the end of a homestay, which phrase thanks your host family for everything?
options: 「どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
「いろいろおせわになりました。」
questions.explanation: 「おせわになりました」 thanks someone for looking after you, the set phrase on leaving a homestay. 「おじゃまします」 is said on entering someone's home, and 「おかえりなさい」 welcomes someone back. 「どうぞよろしくおねがいします」 is for the start of a stay.

questions.stem: How does a student in Japan normally address a teacher called Tanaka?
questions.explanation: 「先生」 is used as a title after the name, and on its own to address the teacher directly. 「さん」 is the general polite suffix, but students do not use it for their teachers.

questions.stem: Which name suffix is the most respectful, used for customers and on envelopes?
questions.explanation: 「さま」 is more formal than 「さん」: 「おきゃくさま」, customer, and 「田中さま」 on a letter. 「くん」 is mostly for boys and younger males, and 「ちゃん」 for small children and close friends.

questions.stem: How do you introduce yourself as Jack to your host family?
options: 「ジャックです。どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
「ジャックさんです。どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
「ジャックさまです。どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
「ジャックくんです。どうぞよろしくおねがいします。」
questions.explanation: Name suffixes show respect for other people, so you never put one on your own name. Your host family will call you 「ジャックさん」 or 「ジャックくん」, but you say only 「ジャックです」.

questions.stem: Talking to your host family about your own mother, which word do you use for her?
questions.explanation: To people outside the family you use the humble 「母」 (はは): 「母は先生です」. 「お母さん」 is for addressing your own mother or talking about someone else's, and 「おばさん」 is an aunt or a woman of your parents' age.

questions.stem: You meet your friend's grandfather for the first time. Which question suits?
options: 「休みの日は何をしていますか。」
questions.explanation: An older person you have just met calls for the polite 「〜ます」 form. The other three are plain forms with casual endings, which suit friends and family your own age.

questions.stem: How does a Japanese personal letter traditionally begin, after the reader's name?
options: With a comment on the season or the weather
With the writer's address and the date
With the reason for writing and a request
With a list of the news the letter will give
questions.explanation: Letters open with a seasonal remark such as 「だんだんさむくなってきましたが、お元気ですか。」 The date and the writer's name traditionally come at the end, after the main text.

questions.stem: What does 「より」 mean after a name at the end of a letter, as in 「ケイトより」?
questions.explanation: A name + 「より」 signs off a letter or email from the writer, and the reader's name + 「へ」 opens it: 「ゆみさんへ」. 「より」 also means 'than' in comparisons, but not after a signature.

questions.stem: Which sentence typically closes a personal letter to a friend?
options: 「お体に気をつけてください。」
questions.explanation: 「お体に気をつけて」, 'take care of yourself', is a usual closing line before signing off. 「お元気ですか」 and 「おひさしぶりです」 belong at the start, and 「はじめまして」 to a first meeting.

questions.stem: In a reply to a Japanese pen pal, which sentence thanks them for their letter?
options: 「お手紙ありがとうございました。」
questions.explanation: 「お手紙ありがとうございました」 is the usual way to begin a reply. The others ask for a letter, say you sent one, or ask whether theirs is coming.
